live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card-skimming code planted on online checkout pages
next.in_short: MageCart is the name for skimmer code that steals card details from online shops. Many groups use it. Reports describe thousands of infected sites, a Newegg breach, a supply-chain hit on Volusion and new ways to hide the code.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says several groups use the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Malpedia's reference list names Magecart Groups 4, 8 and 12, FIN6 and Mirrorthief, among others. These names come from the titles of linked articles.
eSentire says FIN7 is one of many cyber gangs observed taking part in Magecart attacks.
WIRED reported in 2019 that Magecart hackers were casting the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.
Trend Micro lists victims across retail, an airline, a ticketing site and online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada.
A headline in Malpedia's references reports campaigns that infected 311 restaurants through online ordering platforms.
ANY.RUN reports a Magecart-style campaign aimed mostly at retail e-commerce sites, with victims in at least 12 countries. ANY.RUN says banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
Malpedia says the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It copies card data from input fields and sends it to command and control servers.

Trend Micro describes three tactics: infecting third-party companies that supply code to other sites, scanning the internet for unsecured servers, and writing skimming code that works across many payment pages.
Malwarebytes found skimmers hosted on Heroku. A single injected line loads remote JavaScript, a rogue iframe overlays the payment form, and the stolen data goes back in encoded form.
Sucuri tied the ATMZOW skimmer to Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 the actors used 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
ANY.RUN describes checkout hijacking, imitation payment pages, heavy obfuscation and WebSocket exfiltration of card data.
Sansec reports a Linux trojan, CronRAT, that hides in scheduled tasks set for February 31st. Sansec says it enables server-side Magecart data theft.
WIRED reported that, by its account, the group hit 17,000 domains in a few months, and named British Airways and Ticketmaster among past hacks.

RiskIQ reported that attackers registered a lookalike domain on August 13th and put a skimmer on Newegg's payment page around August 14th. It was removed on September 18th, so customers were exposed for over a month.
RiskIQ said the Newegg skimmer reused code recognisable from the British Airways incident.
In October 2019 hackers breached Volusion, a provider of cloud-hosted online stores. The report says more than 6,500 stores were affected and calls it a classic Magecart supply-chain attack.
ANY.RUN reports a campaign active for at least 24 months and supported by over 100 domains. The same injected code was also used to push an Android APK.
Shop owners should check regularly for scripts on payment pages that they did not add, and treat any unexpected one as a sign of compromise.
Banks should watch for fraud on cards used at shops known to have been hit.
